title: Just Use Redis — Redis-Centric Systems Design
description: Design a social e-commerce app (browse, cart, checkout, trending, and retention analytics) that leans on Redis for almost every hot path. The organizing idea: each core feature maps to the Redis data structure that fits it best — Strings for sessions/cache/locks, Integers (INCR) for counters/rate limits/IDs, Hashes for the cart, Sorted Sets for leaderboards, Lists for a work queue, and Bitmaps for daily-active-user retention — all backed by a durable system of record.

nodes.label: Web / Mobile App
nodes.description: Shopper's browser or mobile app; logs in, browses, adds to cart, checks out.

nodes.label: API Gateway / LB
nodes.description: Terminates TLS, authenticates the session cookie, and routes to the app tier.

nodes.label: Application Service
nodes.description: Stateless business logic; reads and writes Redis and the database.

nodes.label: Redis — Strings (Sessions/Cache/Lock)
nodes.description: String keys: session tokens, cached product JSON, and SET NX distributed locks.

nodes.label: Redis — Integers (Counters/RateLimit/ID)
nodes.description: Integer keys via INCR: view counters, rate-limit windows, and a global ID generator.

nodes.label: Redis — Hashes (Cart)
nodes.description: One hash per user (cart:{uid}) mapping product_id -> quantity.

nodes.label: Redis — Sorted Sets (Leaderboard)
nodes.description: ZSETs scored by sales/views for trending products and seller leaderboards.

nodes.label: Async Queue (Streams / List / Broker)
nodes.description: The async work queue for order confirmation emails and fulfillment jobs. Recommended default: Redis Streams (consumer groups, XACK, PEL) or an external broker; a hardened Redis List is the simpler variant. Fed by the DB outbox after commit.

nodes.label: Redis — Bitmaps (Retention)
nodes.description: One bitmap per day (dau:{date}); SETBIT user_id marks a user active for DAU/retention.

nodes.label: Async Worker
nodes.description: Pops jobs from the Redis list and sends emails / triggers fulfillment.

nodes.label: System of Record (RDBMS)
nodes.description: Durable source of truth for users, products, and committed orders.

nodes.label: Metrics & Alerting
nodes.description: Tracks hit rate, memory, evictions, queue depth, replica lag; drives alerts.

functional: Authenticate users and keep a login session across requests.
Browse products fast, serving hot product data from cache.
Add/update/remove items in a per-user shopping cart.
Count product views and enforce per-user rate limits.
Generate globally unique order IDs without a DB round trip.
Show trending products and seller leaderboards ranked in real time.
Process order confirmations and fulfillment asynchronously.
Report daily-active users and N-day retention.
nonFunctional: Sub-millisecond reads on hot paths, with a low p99 under load.
Read-heavy: browses and cart reads vastly outnumber writes.
Durable for money-critical data (orders): RPO 0 — committed orders survive any Redis failover because the RDBMS is authoritative.
Available across a node failure with per-family RPO: sessions/queue tolerate seconds of loss (async replication); orders tolerate none.
Memory-bounded: the working set must fit RAM with a clear eviction story.

capacity.label: Peak business reads/sec
capacity.note: Browse, cart reads, session lookups — mostly served from Redis.

capacity.label: Peak business writes/sec
capacity.note: Cart edits, rate-limit windows, cart -> order commits — the durable/state-changing writes, NOT counting derived view counters (see below).

capacity.label: Derived Redis writes/sec
capacity.note: Every product read INCRs a view counter, so browsing alone can drive up to ~200k counter writes/s — unless view counts are sampled or locally aggregated and flushed with periodic INCRBY (see Step 3), which cuts this to a small fraction. Size shards for the higher of the raw or batched rate.

capacity.label: Active sessions
capacity.note: String keys with TTL; ~1 KB each ≈ 10 GB.

capacity.label: Cart hashes
capacity.note: Hash per active cart; small, TTL'd for abandonment.

capacity.label: Ops per product read
capacity.note: session GET + product GET + view INCR; +1 DB read/backfill only on a cache miss. At 200k reads/s that's ~400–600k Redis ops/s just for browse.

capacity.label: Redis memory (by family)
capacity.note: sessions ~10 GB (10M×1 KB) + product cache ~20–40 GB (hot set) + carts ~5–10 GB (5M small hashes) + ranking/counters a few GB + queue/bitmaps small. Round up ~2× for fragmentation + replication buffers.

capacity.label: Queue throughput + backlog
capacity.note: If workers stall 5 min at ~1 KB/job, backlog ≈ 10k×300×1 KB ≈ 3 GB — bound it and alert; shed or spill low-priority jobs before it grows unbounded.

capacity.label: Replica + AOF overhead
capacity.note: Each replica holds a full copy, so 2 replicas ≈ 3× the RAM above. AOF (appendfsync everysec) adds sequential write load ≈ the write rate × record size; RDB forks briefly double RSS via copy-on-write.

capacity.label: Shards / replicas
capacity.note: ~180 GB working set / ~25–30 GB usable per node ≈ 6–10 primary shards for RAM headroom; +2 replicas each for failover. Also size for ops throughput, not just RAM: browse ops (~400–600k/s) plus derived counter writes push total ops well past what one primary handles, which is a second reason to shard. Split evictable cache keys from non-evictable sessions/queue/carts across separate clusters.

capacity.label: DAU bitmap size
capacity.note: One bit per user; 10M users ≈ 1.25 MB per daily key — cheap retention (assumes dense user_id offsets).

api.description: Authenticate and create a session; returns a session cookie.
Fetch a product; served from the string cache on a hit, DB + backfill on a miss. Also INCRs the view counter.
Read the current cart; HGETALL on the user's cart hash.
Add or update a cart line; HSET on the user's cart hash. qty:0 removes the line (equivalent to DELETE). Validated against the live catalog and capped at a max line count.
Remove a cart line; HDEL on the user's cart hash.

Idempotent checkout. Requires an Idempotency-Key header. Takes a cart lock (latency guard, not the correctness boundary), then in one DB transaction inserts the idempotency row (unique constraint), the order + order_items with snapshotted prices, and an outbox job; a dispatcher enqueues to Redis after commit. A retry with the same key returns the existing order.
Top-N trending products for a window/category/seller dimension; reads the matching ZSET key (e.g. trending:day:{category}).

Admin/reporting endpoint for DAU and N-day retention over the daily bitmaps; BITCOUNT for DAU, BITOP AND + BITCOUNT for N-day retention. Auth-gated; honors the data-retention window on old daily keys.

dataModel.name: session (String)
dataModel.note: Key sid:{token} -> user + metadata JSON, TTL.

dataModel.name: product cache (String)
dataModel.note: Key prod:{id} -> serialized product, TTL + jitter.

dataModel.name: order queue (Stream / List)
dataModel.note: queue:orders holds serialized async jobs, fed by the DB outbox. Recommended: a Redis Stream consumed by a consumer group (XADD/XREADGROUP/XACK); a List (LPUSH/BRPOPLPUSH) is the simpler variant.

fields.name: entry
fields.type: json { orderId, userId, type } (Stream entry or List element)

dataModel.name: dau (Bitmap)
dataModel.note: dau:{date} bit at offset user_id = active.

dataModel.name: orders (RDBMS)
dataModel.note: Durable order record and its state machine. States: created -> paid -> queued -> fulfilled, or failed. The created -> paid transition is driven by payment authorization/capture and inventory reservation, which are out of scope here (see the Step 4 scope note) but would be durable rows in this same DB. Redis never owns this.

dataModel.name: order_items (RDBMS)
dataModel.note: One row per line, with the price snapshotted at checkout — the durable counterpart of the ephemeral Redis cart hash.

dataModel.name: checkout_idempotency (RDBMS)
dataModel.note: Makes order creation exactly-once per idempotency key (effectively-once from the client's view). Unique constraint on idempotency_key; a retry finds the row and returns the same order.

dataModel.name: outbox_jobs (RDBMS)
dataModel.note: Transactional outbox written in the same TX as the order; a dispatcher LPUSHes/XADDs to Redis after commit and marks dispatched. Source of truth for pending async work.

technologyChoices.concern: API gateway, load balancing, and request admission
tradeoff: Keep the edge layer stateless: TLS termination, coarse admission control, routing, health checks, and request-size limits belong here.
Per-user sessions, fine-grained rate counters, cart state, and locks still belong in Redis or the database so the edge does not become a hidden state store.
technologyChoices.makesIrrelevant: A managed edge service with health checks, WAF integration, and autoscaling removes most hand-built reverse-proxy failover and L7 load-balancer operations.

technologyChoices.concern: Redis-compatible hot key-value tier for sessions, cache, and locks
tradeoff: Self-hosted Redis-compatible stores give tight control over eviction, persistence, modules, and version rollout.
Managed Redis-compatible services remove most node replacement, patching, failover, and backup operations, but you still own key design, memory sizing, and client retry behavior.
Use Redis locks only as duplicate-work guards; correctness for checkout remains in the durable idempotency row.
technologyChoices.makesIrrelevant: A managed multi-AZ Redis service removes most Sentinel/failover automation, but it does not remove the need to split evictable cache keys from non-evictable sessions, carts, and queues.

technologyChoices.concern: Atomic counters, rate limits, and global ID allocation
tradeoff: Redis-compatible INCR is the lowest-latency fit for view counters, fixed-window limits, and request IDs when bounded failover loss is acceptable.
Durable databases or conditional-write key-value stores are better when the counter itself is a correctness boundary rather than derived state.
For product views, local aggregation and periodic INCRBY can reduce the derived Redis write rate by orders of magnitude.
technologyChoices.makesIrrelevant: A store with native atomic increment plus TTL support removes app-side read-modify-write counters and most cleanup jobs for expiring rate-limit windows.

technologyChoices.concern: Mutable cart state and checkout idempotency boundary
tradeoff: Redis hashes are ideal for hot, abandoned-cart state because line-item mutations are atomic and cheap.
The checkout idempotency key, order rows, and outbox need a durable transaction or conditional write, not an in-memory lock.
A durable key-value store can own carts directly, but usually adds read latency and cost to the highest-volume path.
technologyChoices.makesIrrelevant: A transactional database with a unique idempotency key removes the need to make a Redis lock responsible for exactly-once order creation.

tradeoff: Sorted sets are the right fit when the product needs fresh top-N reads with incremental score updates.
For long-horizon analytics, backfill a warehouse from events; do not make Redis the only copy of historical ranking inputs.
Very large multi-dimensional leaderboards need careful key partitioning, score decay, and TTL windows to avoid unbounded memory growth.
technologyChoices.makesIrrelevant: A managed Redis-compatible cluster removes most node operations for leaderboard shards, but not the need to design windowed keys and memory caps.

tradeoff: Redis Streams or a broker fit the order path because acknowledgements, replay, consumer groups, and lag metrics are built in.
A Redis List is simpler for fire-and-forget work, but durable delivery requires a processing list, reaper, retry counters, and dead-letter handling.
Managed queues reduce broker operations, but workers still need idempotent side effects because delivery remains at-least-once.
technologyChoices.makesIrrelevant: A managed queue with native DLQ, visibility timeout, consumer scaling, and lag metrics removes most hand-built BRPOPLPUSH recovery code.

tradeoff: Redis bitmaps are extremely compact for dense user IDs and short DAU or retention windows.
A warehouse or analytical store is better for long retention history, ad hoc dimensions, and privacy-governed reporting.
Approximate cardinality sketches reduce memory for unique counts, but they cannot answer exact N-day intersection questions as directly as bitmaps.
technologyChoices.makesIrrelevant: An event pipeline into a warehouse removes many long-window bitmap calculations from Redis, while keeping Redis bitmaps for hot exact daily counters.

technologyChoices.concern: Durable system of record, idempotency, and transactional outbox
tradeoff: A relational database is the cleanest fit for order, order_items, idempotency, and outbox rows because one transaction defines the correctness boundary.
A conditional-write key-value store can work when the order model is simple, but cross-entity invariants and reporting joins become harder.
Redis should accelerate and coordinate; the DB owns RPO 0 for committed money state.
technologyChoices.makesIrrelevant: A managed HA database with backups, point-in-time restore, and read replicas removes much of the custom database failover and backup plumbing around the order path.

technologyChoices.concern: Redis persistence, replication, clustering, and memory governance
tradeoff: Self-hosting gives full control over AOF/RDB policy, shard count, hash tags, eviction policy, and maintenance windows.
Managed Redis-compatible services simplify failover, replacement, patching, and backups, but still require careful memory sizing and client-side resilience.
Separate clusters or databases by durability class: evictable product cache should not share eviction policy with carts, sessions, queues, and counters.
technologyChoices.makesIrrelevant: A managed Redis cluster removes most Sentinel, backup scheduling, and node-replacement code, but not key-family isolation or capacity planning.

technologyChoices.concern: Operational visibility for Redis and async paths
tradeoff: Self-hosted observability gives maximum control over retention, labels, and dashboards, but it becomes another stateful platform to run.
Cloud-native monitoring integrates quickly with managed Redis, queues, and databases, but cross-cloud or self-hosted Redis visibility may require custom exporters.
Alert on symptoms tied to the interview design: memory fragmentation, evictions, hit rate, p99, queue age, retry/DLQ rate, AOF fsync latency, and replica lag.
technologyChoices.makesIrrelevant: Managed telemetry with Redis and queue integrations removes much of the custom scraping and dashboard plumbing, but not SLO definition or incident runbooks.

steps.title: 1. Naive: One RDBMS for Everything (the baseline)
description: Start with the simplest thing that works: a single relational database backs every feature. Sessions live in a sessions table, the cart in a cart table, product reads are SELECTs, view counts are UPDATE ... SET views = views + 1, trending is an ORDER BY over an aggregate, and background emails are sent inline during the checkout request.

It's correct and easy to reason about, and it makes the bottlenecks obvious. Every product view is a disk-backed read and a row UPDATE; the counter UPDATE serializes on a single hot row; ranking is a heavy sort over a growing table on every page load; and sending email inline makes checkout slow and fragile.
Each of those pains maps cleanly to a Redis data structure that removes it — which is exactly the tour the next steps take.

view.caption: Everything — sessions, cart, views, ranking, email — runs through one relational database.

steps.decisionPrompt: At 200k reads/sec, what happens to the DB when every product view is a SELECT plus a counter UPDATE on a hot row?
whyNow: The single-DB baseline makes each Redis use case land as a targeted fix rather than 'add Redis because it's fast'.

recap.after: All features work against one RDBMS.
recap.newRisk: Hot reads, serialized counter updates, heavy ranking sorts, and inline email overwhelm the DB and slow every request.

traps.trap: Shipping the single-DB design as good enough.
traps.why: Session lookups, per-view counter updates, and per-request ranking sorts saturate the DB long before the business scales.
traps.instead: Move each hot path onto the Redis structure that fits it, keeping the DB as the durable record.

tradeoffs.name: One store vs. fit-for-purpose stores
tradeoffs.description: A single RDBMS backing every feature is correct and easy to reason about, but it forces every product view through a disk-backed SELECT plus a hot-row counter UPDATE, every trending page through a heavy sort, and checkout through inline email — one engine straining to serve workloads with very different shapes.
tradeoffs.chosen: The design keeps the RDBMS as the durable system of record but treats it as a baseline whose bottlenecks map cleanly onto purpose-built Redis structures for each hot path.

steps.title: 2. Strings — Sessions, Cache, and a Distributed Lock
description: The Redis String is the workhorse: an opaque value under a key, with an optional TTL. Three idiomatic uses cover most of the read path.

Sessions: on login, SET sid:{token} to the user JSON with EXPIRE (a sliding TTL). The token must be a long random value, delivered in a Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite cookie, rotated on privilege change, and revocable by DEL; never derive it from user data. The gateway validates the cookie with one GET instead of a DB query per request.
Cache-aside: product reads GET prod:{id}; on a miss, load from the DB and SET with a short TTL plus jitter (so keys don't all expire together). Hot products now serve from memory.

Distributed lock: SET lock:{resource} {token} NX EX 10 acquires a lock only if absent, auto-expiring so a crashed holder can't deadlock. Release by deleting only if the token matches (a small Lua script) so you never delete someone else's lock. This reduces duplicate concurrent work on checkout — a fast double-submit hits a held lock. But it is not the correctness boundary: if the holder pauses (GC, slow disk) past the 10s expiry, a second request can acquire the same lock and both proceed. Idempotent, exactly-once-per-key order creation comes from a durable idempotency key in the DB with a unique constraint (Step 4 / final design), not the lock. Redis coordinates and accelerates; the DB owns correctness for money.

view.caption: Strings back sessions and a product cache-aside layer, plus SET NX locks; the DB is only touched on a cache miss or a durable write.

steps.decisionPrompt: What's the failure mode of a distributed lock with no expiry, and how does SET NX EX fix it?

concepts.definition: Set a key only if it doesn't exist, with an expiry, atomically.
concepts.whyItMatters: Gives a self-healing distributed lock: a crashed holder's lock expires instead of deadlocking.
concepts.example: SET lock:cart:42 tok NX EX 10 -> guards the checkout critical section.

concepts.definition: Expire cache entries after a bounded, randomized time.
concepts.whyItMatters: Bounds staleness and prevents a synchronized expiry stampede onto the DB.

concepts.description: GET/SET strings for sessions and cached JSON; SET NX EX as a distributed lock.
concepts.whyItMatters: Login sessions, hot read cache, and guarding a critical section like checkout.

whyNow: Sessions and cache are the highest-volume reads; fixing them first removes most DB read load before anything else.

recap.before: Sessions and product reads hit the DB every request.
recap.after: Sessions, hot products, and a checkout lock all live in Redis strings.
recap.newRisk: Counting and ID generation still hammer hot DB rows — the next fix is atomic integers.

traps.trap: A lock with no expiry (or DEL without a token check).
traps.why: A crashed holder deadlocks the resource; a blind DEL can release a lock a different request now holds.
traps.instead: SET NX EX for auto-release, and release with a compare-and-delete Lua script.

flows.name: Product read — string cache-aside
flows.note: A hit returns from memory; a miss loads from the DB and backfills the string with a jittered TTL.

tradeoffs.name: Lock liveness vs. lock safety
tradeoffs.description: A distributed lock with no expiry deadlocks the resource forever when its holder crashes, while adding a TTL (SET NX EX) means a slow-but-alive holder can lose the lock mid-work; the atomic set-with-expiry trades a small false-expiry risk for guaranteed eventual release.
tradeoffs.chosen: The design uses SET NX EX so a dead holder can never block the resource permanently, accepting that TTL choice becomes a tuning concern.

tradeoffs.name: Cache freshness vs. database load
tradeoffs.description: Cache-aside with a short TTL serves hot product reads from memory instead of the DB, but every cached read can be up to one TTL stale, and naive expiry lets many keys lapse together and stampede the database.
tradeoffs.chosen: The design accepts short-TTL staleness on product reads and adds jitter to expiry times, trading perfect freshness for taking the read hot path off the database.

steps.title: 3. Integers — Counters, Rate Limiting, and Global IDs
description: A String that holds a number is a Redis integer, and INCR/INCRBY are atomic — no read-modify-write race, no hot-row lock in the DB.

View counters: INCR views:{productId} on a view. It's a single in-memory op; a background job periodically flushes the totals to the DB so the durable record stays roughly current without paying per-view write cost. At 200k reads/s a naive per-read INCR is 200k extra Redis writes/s (the 'derived Redis writes' line in the capacity table), which dominates write load — so at this scale you sample (INCR 1-in-N and scale up), or aggregate counts per-instance in memory and flush with a periodic INCRBY, or feed views through a stream and aggregate; any of these cuts the counter write rate to a small fraction and keeps shard sizing driven by real business writes.

Rate limiting: a fixed-window limiter is INCR rl:{userId}:{minute} with EXPIRE 60 on first hit; if the value exceeds the limit, reject. Make the INCR-then-EXPIRE atomic on the first hit (a two-line Lua script, or SET NX EX to seed the window) so a crash between the two commands can't leave a window with no TTL that blocks the user forever. Note fixed windows are bursty at the boundary — a client can spend a full quota at :59 and another at :00; a sliding-window or token-bucket variant (also a short Lua script) smooths that. This throttles abusive clients before they reach the DB.

Global unique IDs: INCR order:id returns a monotonic counter shared across all app instances — a DB-free ID generator. Hand out ranges (INCRBY 1000) per instance to cut round trips, or seed the counter high to reserve a namespace. Treat this as an order-request id, not proof of a committed order: the durable DB row (with a unique idempotency key) is what makes order creation idempotent — exactly-once per idempotency key — while the async work stays at-least-once.

view.caption: INCR drives view counts, rate-limit windows, and a global ID generator; totals flush to the DB in the background.

steps.decisionPrompt: Why is INCR safe under concurrency where SELECT ... then UPDATE ... +1 in the app is not?

concepts.definition: Increment a key's integer value in a single atomic command.
concepts.whyItMatters: No lost updates under concurrency and no hot-row contention in the DB.

concepts.definition: Count requests per user per time bucket and reject over a threshold.
concepts.whyItMatters: Cheap abuse protection at the edge of the app, before load reaches the DB.

concepts.definition: A shared monotonic INCR counter as a unique-ID source.
concepts.whyItMatters: Generates unique order IDs without a DB sequence round trip; ranges cut chatter.
concepts.example: INCRBY order:id 1000 -> reserve a block per instance.

concepts.description: Single-command atomic increment for counts, windows, and IDs.
concepts.whyItMatters: View counts, rate limiting, and generating monotonic unique IDs.

whyNow: Counting and ID generation are the write-side twin of step 2's read caching — both remove hot-row DB pressure.

recap.before: Counts and IDs contended on hot DB rows/sequences.
recap.after: Atomic INCR handles views, rate limits, and unique IDs in memory.
recap.newRisk: The cart is still a relational table with a row per line — a structure Redis models better as a hash.

traps.why: Two concurrent requests read the same value and both write value+1, losing an increment.
traps.instead: Use atomic INCR/INCRBY so the increment happens server-side in one step.

flows.name: Rate limit + view count
flows.note: One INCR enforces the per-user window; another counts the view — both atomic and DB-free.

tradeoffs.name: Count exactness vs. write volume
tradeoffs.description: A per-view INCR is atomic and exact, but at 200k reads/s it adds 200k derived Redis writes/s that dominate write load; sampling (INCR 1-in-N and scale up) or per-instance aggregation with periodic INCRBY slashes that load at the cost of approximate or slightly delayed counts.
tradeoffs.chosen: The design accepts approximate view counts at scale — sampled or batch-aggregated — because a display counter does not justify making counter writes the system's biggest write workload.

tradeoffs.name: In-memory speed vs. durable record
tradeoffs.description: Keeping the live counter in Redis makes each increment a single in-memory op with no hot-row lock, but Redis is not the durable record; periodically flushing totals to the DB keeps the durable copy roughly current without paying a durable write per view.
tradeoffs.chosen: The design counts in Redis and flushes to the DB in the background, trading real-time durability of the counter for removing per-view write cost from the database.

steps.title: 4. Hashes — The Shopping Cart
description: A cart is a small map of product_id -> quantity owned by one user — exactly a Redis Hash. Store it as cart:{uid} with HSET product_id qty.

Field-level operations are the win: HSET to add/update one line, HINCRBY to bump a quantity, HDEL to remove a line, HGETALL to render the cart, HLEN for a badge count — all without serializing and rewriting the whole object as you would with a single JSON string.
Set a TTL on the cart key so abandoned carts expire automatically (abandonment analytics can snapshot them first).

Cap the cart (HLEN limit) and validate each product_id against the live catalog before adding, so the Redis cart can't drift from real products. The cart holds only product_id -> qty; do NOT trust a client-supplied price. At checkout, HGETALL reads the cart, the app snapshots the current price per line from the catalog, and writes durable order_items rows to the DB inside the order transaction — the Redis cart is ephemeral input, the DB order_items are the record. Idempotency lives here too: that same transaction inserts a checkout_idempotency row keyed by the client's Idempotency-Key with a unique constraint, so a retried checkout returns the existing order instead of creating a second one.
Hashes are also memory-efficient: small hashes use a compact encoding, so millions of little carts stay cheap.

Scope note: payment authorization/capture and inventory reservation are out of scope for this Redis-focused chapter. In a real checkout they would sit in the same DB transaction (or a saga) — e.g. payment_authorizations and inventory_reservations rows — and gate the order's move from created to paid; here we assume that boundary exists and focus on the Redis structures. It matters because that's what actually moves an order to paid and prevents oversell; we call it out so the created -> paid -> fulfilled states aren't ambiguous.

view.caption: Each user's cart is one Redis hash (cart:{uid}) with a field per product; checkout reads it and commits to the DB.

steps.decisionPrompt: Why is a hash better than a single JSON string for a cart that's edited one line at a time?

concepts.definition: Model a mutable object as one hash with a field per attribute.
concepts.whyItMatters: Partial reads/writes (one field) avoid rewriting the whole object and cut contention.
concepts.example: HINCRBY cart:42 p99 1 bumps one line's quantity.

whyNow: The cart is the most-edited per-user object; a hash gives field-level edits the earlier string cache can't.

recap.before: Cart edits were row-level DB writes or whole-object rewrites.
recap.after: The cart is one hash with cheap field-level HSET/HINCRBY/HDEL.
recap.newRisk: Ranking (trending, leaderboards) is still a heavy DB sort per request.

traps.trap: Storing the cart as one JSON string.
traps.why: Every line edit reads, deserializes, mutates, and rewrites the whole value — racy and wasteful.
traps.instead: Use a hash so each line is an independent field updated atomically.

tradeoffs.name: Field-level edits vs. single-blob simplicity
tradeoffs.description: Storing the cart as one JSON string is the simplest representation, but every one-line edit means reading, deserializing, and rewriting the whole object; a Hash costs a slightly richer command vocabulary (HSET, HINCRBY, HDEL, HGETALL) in exchange for touching only the line that changed.
tradeoffs.chosen: The design stores the cart as a Redis Hash because carts are edited one line at a time, making field-level operations the natural unit of work.

tradeoffs.name: Auto-expiry convenience vs. cart retention
tradeoffs.description: A TTL on the cart key makes abandoned carts clean themselves up with zero housekeeping code, but it also means a returning shopper can find an empty cart and abandonment data vanishes unless analytics snapshots it before expiry.
tradeoffs.chosen: The design puts a TTL on cart keys and lets abandonment analytics snapshot carts first, preferring automatic cleanup over indefinitely accumulating stale carts.

steps.title: 5. Sorted Sets — Trending & Leaderboards
description: Ranking wants the top-N by score, updated continuously. A Redis Sorted Set (ZSET) keeps members ordered by a float score, so 'top 10 trending products' or 'top sellers this week' is a ZREVRANGE that costs O(log n + m) — the log to find the start plus m for the m items returned. Keep m small (top-10, not top-10k) and this stays cheap; a full ZRANGE 0 -1 is O(n) and defeats the point.
Update on the fly: ZINCRBY trending {weight} {productId} on a view or sale nudges a product's score; ZREVRANGE trending 0 9 WITHSCORES reads the leaderboard instantly — no sort over a growing table.

Time-decay keeps 'trending' fresh: either periodically multiply scores down, or bucket by window (trending:{hour}) and ZUNIONSTORE recent buckets with decaying weights. ZREMRANGEBYRANK trims the set so it can't grow unbounded.
The same structure powers any leaderboard: sellers by revenue, products by rating, users by points — all ZADD/ZINCRBY writes and ZRANGE/ZRANK reads.

view.caption: Trending and leaderboards are Redis sorted sets: ZINCRBY on activity, ZREVRANGE to read the top-N in log time.

steps.decisionPrompt: How does a ZSET turn a per-request ORDER BY over a growing table into an O(log n + m) top-N read?

concepts.definition: A set of members each with a float score, kept in score order.
concepts.whyItMatters: Top-N reads are O(log n + m) (logarithmic seek plus the m returned items) and rank queries O(log n), with no table sort, and updates are incremental.
concepts.example: ZINCRBY trending 1 p99 then ZREVRANGE trending 0 9.

concepts.definition: Reduce old scores over time so 'trending' reflects recent activity.
concepts.whyItMatters: Keeps rankings current without a full recompute.
concepts.example: Windowed keys trending:{hour} combined with decaying weights via ZUNIONSTORE.

concepts.description: ZADD scores and ZREVRANGE for real-time ranking.
concepts.whyItMatters: Trending products, seller leaderboards, top-N of anything.

whyNow: Ranking was the last heavy per-request DB sort; a ZSET makes it an incremental in-memory read.

recap.after: Ranking is incremental ZINCRBY writes and O(log n + m) ZREVRANGE top-N reads.
recap.newRisk: Checkout still sends email inline, and we have no cheap way to measure DAU/retention.

traps.trap: Recomputing ranking with ORDER BY on every request.
traps.why: The sort cost grows with the table and dominates read latency at scale.
traps.instead: Maintain a ZSET incrementally and read the top-N directly.

flows.name: Update + read trending
flows.note: Activity nudges scores with ZINCRBY; the leaderboard read is a single range query.

tradeoffs.name: Write-time ranking vs. read-time sorting
tradeoffs.description: The RDBMS approach re-sorts a growing aggregate table on every trending page load; a ZSET instead pays O(log n) on every ZINCRBY at write time so the top-10 read is a cheap O(log n + m) ZREVRANGE — moving the sort cost from the read path to the far more tolerant write path.
tradeoffs.chosen: The design maintains rank continuously in a sorted set, paying per-update log cost so leaderboard reads are effectively free at any traffic level.

tradeoffs.name: Trending freshness vs. score history
tradeoffs.description: Raw cumulative scores let old hits dominate trending forever; time-decay (periodic multiply-down) or windowed buckets keep the board fresh but deliberately forget history and add a maintenance job or extra keys.
tradeoffs.chosen: The design applies time-decay or window bucketing so trending reflects what is hot now, accepting that long-run popularity must be tracked elsewhere.

steps.title: 6. Lists & Bitmaps — Work Queue and Retention
description: Two more structures close out the tour: Lists for async work and Bitmaps for cheap analytics.

List as a queue: instead of sending order email inline, the app LPUSHes a job onto queue:orders and returns immediately; a pool of workers BRPOPs (blocking pop) and processes jobs — emails, fulfillment, inventory updates. This decouples checkout latency from slow side effects.

The enqueue itself is the sharp edge. A bare LPUSH after the DB commit can be lost if the app crashes between commit and push, or duplicated if the push succeeds but the response is lost and the client retries. Make it a transactional outbox: the checkout DB transaction writes the order AND an outbox_jobs row atomically, and a dispatcher (polling the outbox or a CDC stream) LPUSHes to Redis after commit and marks the row dispatched. Now the DB is the source of truth for pending work; Redis is a fast delivery buffer that can be rebuilt from the outbox.

Hardening the List into a real queue takes machinery Redis doesn't give for free: BRPOPLPUSH (or BLMOVE) into a per-worker processing list so an in-flight job survives a worker crash; a reaper that scans processing lists and re-queues jobs older than a visibility timeout; a retry count with exponential backoff; a dead-letter list for poison messages that exceed max retries; a bounded backlog with an alert (and admission control / shedding low-priority jobs) when workers fall behind; and worker idempotency keyed on jobId/orderId so a redelivered job is a no-op. At ~10k jobs/s with a no-drop requirement, this is the minimum — which is exactly why the option comparison below leans toward Streams/a broker when you want these guarantees built in.

Bitmap for retention: a bitmap is a string addressed at the bit level. Keep one key per day, dau:{date}, and SETBIT dau:{date} {userId} 1 when a user is active. BITCOUNT dau:{date} gives that day's active users; BITOP AND over consecutive days (then BITCOUNT) gives N-day retention — a bit over a megabyte per day for 10M users. This assumes dense, small integer user IDs: SETBIT at offset 5,000,000,000 allocates a 625 MB string, so a bitmap needs a compact user_id -> offset mapping, not a raw UUID. If you only need approximate distinct counts (DAU without per-user retention math), a HyperLogLog (PFADD/PFCOUNT) is ~12 KB regardless of user count and sidesteps the offset problem — trade exactness for size. Retention data is user-level activity; apply your retention/privacy policy (expire old daily keys, honor deletion requests) rather than keeping bitmaps forever.
Between them, Lists give ordered producer/consumer work and Bitmaps give set-membership analytics at one bit per user.

view.caption: The outbox feeds an async queue (Streams/broker recommended, List as the simpler variant) that workers consume, ack, and complete; SETBIT on a daily bitmap tracks active users for DAU and retention.

options.name: Redis Streams / dedicated broker (recommended)
options.description: Use Redis Streams (consumer groups, acks, PEL) or an external broker like Kafka/SQS for the order path, fed by the DB outbox. This is the recommended default at ~10k jobs/s with a no-drop requirement.
pros: Consumer groups, acknowledgements (XACK), and replay are built in — the delivery guarantees the order path needs.
XAUTOCLAIM/PEL give native visibility-timeout reclaim and a dead-letter path instead of hand-rolled reapers.
Better backpressure and observability, and scales to many partitions/consumers without hand-rolled coordination.
cons: More moving parts and operational surface than a plain list.
An external broker adds another system to run and secure.
Still needs worker idempotency — delivery is at-least-once, not exactly-once.

view.caption: The order path as Streams/consumer-groups (or an external broker), fed by the DB outbox; XACK/PEL give reclaim and dead-lettering.

options.name: Hardened List queue (LPUSH/BRPOPLPUSH)
options.description: A Redis list as a producer/consumer queue with blocking pop — fine for low-stakes fire-and-forget work, but for the order path it needs processing lists, a reaper, retries, and a dead-letter list bolted on by hand.
pros: Dead simple to start: LPUSH to enqueue, BRPOP to block-and-consume — no extra infrastructure.
Very low latency and high throughput for fire-and-forget jobs.
BRPOPLPUSH gives an at-least-once processing list for crash recovery.
cons: No built-in consumer groups, acks, or replay — you build every delivery guarantee yourself.
A slow consumer lets the list grow unbounded and eat memory; needs a bounded backlog + admission control.
No native retry/dead-letter/visibility-timeout; a reaper, retry counters, and a DLQ list are all hand-rolled.

view.caption: A list is the queue: App LPUSHes, Worker BRPOPLPUSHes into a processing list and persists, then LREMs on success.

steps.decisionPrompt: At ~10k jobs/s with a no-drop requirement, do you harden a Redis List (processing list, reaper, retries, DLQ) or reach for Streams / a broker that gives those for free?

concepts.definition: LPUSH to enqueue and (B)RPOP to dequeue, optionally via BRPOPLPUSH.
concepts.whyItMatters: Decouples slow side effects from the request path with almost no infrastructure.

concepts.definition: A bit per entity in a string, addressed with SETBIT/BITCOUNT/BITOP.
concepts.whyItMatters: DAU and N-day retention for millions of users in a few KB per day.

concepts.description: LPUSH producers, BRPOP consumers for async jobs.
concepts.whyItMatters: Order emails, fulfillment, any fire-and-forget background work.

whyNow: These remove the last inline side effect (email) and add analytics the earlier structures couldn't express cheaply.

recap.before: Email was inline and DAU/retention had no cheap representation.
recap.after: An outbox-fed queue (Streams recommended, or a hardened List) offloads side effects with retry/DLQ semantics; daily bitmaps make DAU/retention trivial.
recap.newRisk: Now that orders, sessions, and the queue all live in Redis, a node loss or full disk is a data-loss and availability problem — persistence and HA come next.

traps.trap: Enqueuing order work with a bare LPUSH right after the DB commit.
traps.why: A crash between commit and LPUSH loses the job; a lost response makes the client retry and duplicate it — the queue and the order state drift.
traps.instead: Write the job to a DB outbox in the same transaction as the order, dispatch to Redis after commit, and make workers idempotent on jobId/orderId.

traps.trap: Treating a plain list queue as exactly-once.
traps.why: A worker that crashes mid-job loses it unless the job is held in a processing list until acked, and redelivery duplicates side effects.
traps.instead: BRPOPLPUSH into a per-worker list with a reaper + DLQ (or move to Streams for real acks), and dedupe side effects on jobId.

flows.name: Async job via list queue
flows.note: The job sits in a processing list until the worker finishes, so a crash mid-job is recoverable.

tradeoffs.name: Hand-rolled simplicity vs. built-in delivery guarantees
tradeoffs.description: A bare LPUSH/BRPOP list is dead simple and very fast, but for the no-drop order path you must hand-roll processing lists, a reaper, retry counters, and a dead-letter list; Redis Streams or a broker like Kafka/SQS ship consumer groups, acks, PEL reclaim, and replay out of the box at the cost of more moving parts to run.
tradeoffs.chosen: At ~10k jobs/s with a no-drop requirement the design chooses Streams or a dedicated broker, because the delivery machinery a list forces you to build by hand is exactly what these systems provide natively.

tradeoffs.name: Fast enqueue vs. atomic commit
tradeoffs.description: LPUSHing the job directly after the DB commit is the fastest path, but a crash between commit and push loses the job and a retried push duplicates it; routing the enqueue through a transactional outbox row written in the checkout transaction closes that window at the cost of a relay and an outbox table.
tradeoffs.chosen: The design writes the order and the outbox job in one DB transaction and lets a relay feed the queue, because checkout side effects must be neither lost nor doubled.

steps.title: 7. Scale & Survive — Persistence, HA, and Cluster
description: Once Redis holds sessions, carts, counters, the queue, and analytics, it's no longer a disposable cache — losing it is an outage and, for orders in flight, potential data loss. Three concerns make it production-grade.

Durability: enable AOF (append-only file, fsync every second) and/or RDB snapshots so a restart reloads recent state. Money-critical facts (committed orders) are still written to the durable RDBMS as the true source of record; Redis durability is about not cold-starting sessions/queue on restart.

High availability: run primary + replicas with automatic failover (Sentinel, or Cluster's built-in failover / a managed service). Clients reconnect and reads can fan out to replicas. Because replication is asynchronous, a failover can lose the last few writes, so define RPO per key family: a view counter tolerates seconds of loss (RPO ~seconds), a session or a queued job tolerates a little, but a committed order tolerates none (RPO 0) — which is exactly why that fact lives in the durable RDBMS and the outbox, not in Redis alone.

Sharding for memory + throughput: Redis Cluster hash-slots the keyspace across nodes so total RAM and ops/sec scale horizontally. Keep keys that must be operated on together (a Lua lock + counter, MULTI over one cart) in the same slot using hash tags like cart:{uid}. Watch memory: set maxmemory + an eviction policy for the pure-cache keys (product cache) while protecting non-evictable keys (sessions, queue) — often by separating them into different logical instances.

view.caption: The full platform: every Redis structure in play, backed by a durable RDBMS, made highly available with replication/failover and scaled with cluster sharding.

steps.decisionPrompt: Which Redis keys can you safely evict under memory pressure, and which must never be evicted?

concepts.definition: Append-only log of writes vs periodic point-in-time snapshots.
concepts.whyItMatters: Controls how much state a restart recovers and the durability/latency trade-off.
concepts.example: AOF everysec for near-durability; RDB for fast reloads and backups.

concepts.definition: Force related keys into one cluster slot with {...} in the key.
concepts.whyItMatters: Multi-key ops (Lua, MULTI) require all keys on the same node in Cluster mode.
concepts.example: lock:{cart:42} and cart:{cart:42} share a slot.

concepts.definition: What Redis does when it hits its memory cap.
concepts.whyItMatters: Pure cache keys should be evictable (allkeys-lru); sessions/queue must not be.
concepts.example: Separate cache and durable keyspaces so eviction never drops a session.

whyNow: Having put load-bearing state in Redis, durability, failover, and sharding are what keep it from becoming a single point of failure.

recap.before: Redis was a single, volatile node holding load-bearing state.
recap.after: Persistence, replication/failover, and cluster sharding make it durable, available, and scalable.
recap.newRisk: Operational: replica lag, failover windows, memory pressure, and slot migrations must be watched and rehearsed.

traps.trap: Treating Redis as the sole source of truth for money.
traps.why: Async replication can lose the last writes on failover — unacceptable for committed orders.
traps.instead: Keep the durable RDBMS authoritative for orders; use Redis for speed and derived/ephemeral state.

tradeoffs.name: Persistence overhead vs. restart safety
tradeoffs.description: Once Redis holds sessions, carts, counters, and the queue, a cold restart is an outage; AOF with per-second fsync and RDB snapshots bound that loss to about a second of writes, at the cost of disk I/O and slightly slower writes that a pure cache would never pay.
tradeoffs.chosen: The design enables AOF plus snapshots because this Redis is no longer disposable, while still keeping money-critical facts like committed orders in the durable RDBMS.

tradeoffs.name: Evictable cache vs. must-keep state
tradeoffs.description: Under memory pressure Redis can evict keys, which is fine for cache-aside product entries that reload from the DB but catastrophic for the queue, carts, and sessions that exist nowhere else; one instance cannot safely apply a single eviction policy to both kinds of data.
tradeoffs.chosen: The design separates roles so cache data is evictable and re-derivable while queue, cart, and session keys are never evicted, keeping their source of truth or backing store explicit.

finalDesign.title: Final Design — Redis as the Primary Data Platform
finalDesign.description: Stateless app instances front a Redis data platform where each feature uses the fitting structure — Strings (sessions, cache, locks), Integers (counters, rate limits, IDs), Hashes (cart), Sorted Sets (trending/leaderboards), a queue (async work), Bitmaps (DAU/retention) — with an async worker pool draining the queue and a durable RDBMS as the authoritative record. Redis accelerates and coordinates; the DB owns correctness for money. Checkout is idempotent — exactly-once order creation per idempotency key, effectively-once from the client's view — via a durable idempotency key, and writes order + order_items + an outbox job in one transaction; a dispatcher feeds the queue after commit. The async work stays at-least-once with idempotent worker side effects. For the order path we default to Redis Streams (or a broker) — consumer groups, XACK, and PEL reclaim give the retry/visibility-timeout/dead-letter semantics a 10k-jobs/s no-drop queue needs, which a plain List only gets with hand-rolled machinery; a hardened List is acceptable for low-stakes fire-and-forget work. Workers are idempotent on jobId/orderId and reconcile against the DB. Persistence (AOF everysec + RDB), replication/failover, and cluster sharding make the Redis tier production-grade, with cache-like keys split from non-evictable sessions/queue/carts by durability class. Async replication means a failover can lose the last few writes — fine for a view counter (RPO ~seconds), never for a committed order (RPO 0, which is why the DB is authoritative). Monitor memory, evictions, queue age, retry rate, AOF fsync latency, replica lag, and failover events.

view.caption: Every Redis data structure mapped to the feature it fits best, backed by a durable system of record.

flows.name: Checkout — idempotent, outbox-dispatched
flows.note: The lock only guards duplicate concurrent work; correctness comes from the durable idempotency key. The DB transaction writes order + order_items + an outbox job atomically, and a dispatcher feeds the queue after commit — so no job is lost or duplicated.

functional.requirement: Keep a login session across requests
functional.how: Session token in a string key with sliding TTL; one GET per request.
Cache-aside over string keys with jittered TTL.
One hash per user with field-level HSET/HINCRBY/HDEL.
Atomic INCR for view counters and per-window rate limits.
Shared monotonic INCR counter, optionally ranged.
Sorted sets with ZINCRBY updates and ZREVRANGE reads.
Transactional outbox feeds a queue (Streams recommended, or a hardened List); idempotent workers consume, retry, and dead-letter.

nonFunctional.how: In-memory Redis structures on every hot path.
Orders committed to the RDBMS; Redis persistence for warm recovery.
maxmemory + LRU for cache keys, non-evictable sessions/queue separated.

say: Frame it as a read-heavy social e-commerce app: sessions, browse, cart, checkout, trending, and retention analytics.
State the twist explicitly: Redis is the primary hot-path data platform, with a durable RDBMS as the source of record for money.
Start with one RDBMS for everything and name the bottlenecks: hot reads, serialized counters, per-request ranking sorts, inline email.
Walk each feature onto the fitting structure: Strings (session/cache/lock), Integers (counter/limit/ID), Hashes (cart), Sorted Sets (ranking), Lists (queue), Bitmaps (retention).
For each, say the command and why that structure — e.g. INCR is atomic so no lost updates; ZSET makes top-N O(log n + m).
Close on persistence (AOF/RDB), HA (replica + failover), and cluster sharding, with per-key-family RPO.

Make order creation idempotent (exactly-once per Idempotency-Key, effectively-once to the client): Idempotency-Key + a durable idempotency row + a transactional outbox feeding the queue + idempotent workers for the at-least-once async side — the Redis lock only cuts duplicate concurrent work.
Emphasize what Redis is NOT authoritative for (committed orders) and why: async replication can lose the last writes on failover.

expectations: Uses Redis as a cache and knows GET/SET with TTL.
Maps at least a few features to the right structure (cart = hash, leaderboard = sorted set).
Covers all six structures with correct commands and reasons (INCR atomicity, ZSET top-N, bitmap DAU).
Handles the distributed lock correctly (SET NX EX + compare-and-delete).

Draws the line between Redis and the durable RDBMS for money-critical data, and makes order creation idempotent — exactly-once per idempotency key, with at-least-once async work plus idempotent workers (idempotency key + transactional outbox) — rather than trusting the lock.
Addresses persistence, per-key-family RPO/failover semantics (async replication can lose writes), cluster slots/hash-tags, capacity/shard sizing, and eviction policy split by durability class.

followUps: How do you make the distributed lock correct under clock skew and long GC pauses (fencing tokens, Redlock caveats)?
Fixed-window vs sliding-window vs token-bucket rate limiting — which and why, and how do you make it exact with Lua?
How do you keep the trending sorted set fresh without unbounded growth (time decay, windowed keys, ZREMRANGEBYRANK)?
How do you get at-least-once (or exactly-once) semantics from a Redis list queue, and when do you switch to Streams (consumer groups, XACK, PEL) or Kafka?

How do you make checkout effectively-once end to end — exactly-once order creation per Idempotency-Key via a durable idempotency row, plus a transactional outbox and idempotent workers for the at-least-once async side — when the Redis lock alone can't prove it?
How do you size and shard the Redis cluster, and how do you keep co-accessed keys in the same slot (hash tags)?
What exactly is lost on a failover, and how do you set per-key-family RPO so committed orders stay correct despite async replication?
How do you keep DAU/retention bitmaps correct with sparse or UUID user IDs (offset mapping), and when is a HyperLogLog the better tool?
